title: Come, Draw Nearer! The Shady Field
text:
Come, draw nearer! The shady field,

the grim sky and the cold air

predispose the soul to sadness.

Come, rest your head on my shoulder;

like this, together, very close, my lord.


Let us speak of your love; of that dreamed

love! When desolate winter

reigns everywhere, and pale flee away

illusion and faith, how they warm,

the blessed memories of the past!


Come, draw nearer, my sweet lord...

and while with stubborn effort

the gray mist shakes its colossal crest,

may Chimera pour over us

the impalpable amphora of Dream.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the intimate winter address and the dreamlike final amphora.

title: Fan
text:
The little jackets flame, glittering,

the light over the clothes trembles and slips,

and the banderillas feign pyrotechnics

and the crimson gala capes feign dawns.


The sun burns in the panels of the parasols,

the bugle exhales its howl of death,

and the matador, before charros and mantillas,

offers and dedicates the beast that bellows.

Meanwhile a little lady, all nervous,

covers with her hands her beautiful face


framed by silk and gold ringlets,

and half-opens her slight fingers like a fan,

to see behind that grille, without fear,

how the noble blood of the bull springs forth.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the bullring spectacle framed by the lady's fan-like fingers.

title: 1. The Water Running under the Rain
text:
And the Basalt Buddha Smiled

That

afternoon, in the promenade, mad

with love, my sweet idolized one

offered me

the eglantine of her mouth.


And the basalt Buddha smiled...

Another came afterward, and his

charms

stole her from me; I made an appointment with her, and in the shade

we exchanged epistles

and curls.


And the basalt Buddha smiled...

Today it is a year since the love

lost.

I return to the place and, since I am exhausted

after long walking,

I climb to the top

of the pedestal on which the symbol rests.


Defeated and bloody the day dies,

and in the arms of the basalt

Buddha

the mysterious moon surprises me.
editorial_note: The catalog title differs from the embedded Buddha poem, so the internal heading and body are preserved.

title: Androgyne
text:
For you, for you, I cried out when you arose,

infernal archetype, from deep Erebus,

with your neutral charms, your ephebe face,

your pectoral breasts, and came to me.


Shadow and light, bud and pollen at once you were,

awakening in souls the new crime,

now with virilities of a young god,

now with wilted caresses of a sad woman.


I loved you because, in exchange for naive graces,

you had the supreme aristocracies:

blue blood, shy soul, infertile womb;


because you knew much and loved little,

and were rare synthesis of a mad century

and sickly flowering of an old world.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the fin-de-siecle language of ambivalence while keeping the historical diction of the source.

title: Damiana Is Getting Married
text:
With my bitter thoughts

and with all my misfortunes,

I will make your wedding bouquet,

which will not be of orange blossoms.


My eyes, which anguish

and continual vigil

set alight, will be two wilted

torches for your altar.


The weeping that from my grief

without truce is springing

will anoint your pure brow

as with holy water...


—Sir, do not grieve, your frown

hurts me like a reproach;

—How pale you are, my lord!

—It is that I spent a bad night,

love takes sleep from me...


—And you are leaving!...

—I am leaving, it is late,

they are waiting for me; the temple burns

like a sun! Ease your illness,

sir, and God bless you!

—Damiana, may God keep you...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the wedding bouquet made from grief and the closing farewell dialogue.

title: Deity
text:
As the spark sleeps in the pebble

and the statue in the clay,

in you sleeps divinity.

Only in a constant and strong pain,

at the shock, springs from the inert stone

the lightning of deity.

Do not complain, therefore, of destiny,

for what is divine within you

only arises thanks to it.

Endure, if possible, smiling,

the life that the artist goes on sculpting,

the hard blow of the chisel.


What do bad hours matter to you,

if each hour in your newborn wings

places one more beautiful feather?

You will see the condor in full height,

you will see the sculpture finished,

you will see, soul, you will see...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sculptural argument that pain releases the divine spark.

title: The Whirlwind
text:
To see in all things

the traces of the unknown Spirit;

to contemplate

without cease,

in the transparent mysterious nights,

the holy nakedness of the stars...

To wait!

To wait!

For what? Who knows! Perhaps a future

and undreamed peace... Serene and strong,

to run that sublime

and portentous adventure of death.


Meanwhile, to love everything... and to love nothing,

to smile when there is sun and when there are mists;

to take care that on the harsh journey

the wings do not atrophy, nor any wave

of vile mud soil our feathers.


Soul: such is the best orientation,

such is the instinctive course

shown to us by an interior

star.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the spiritual itinerary of waiting, detachment, and the inner star.

title: There Is No Longer a Human Pain That Is Not My Pain...
text:
"There is no longer a human pain that is not my pain;

no eyes now weep, no soul now anguishes

without my anguishing and weeping;

now my heart is the faithful lamp of every vigil,

oh Christ!

"In vain I search in the deep hiding places of my being

to find some hatred: no one can wound me now

except with pity and love. All are I, I am all,

oh Christ!


"What do evils or goods matter! For me all are goods.

The rosebush has no thorns: for me it only gives roses.

Roses of passion? What does it matter! Roses of heavenly essence,

purple as the blood you shed for us,

oh Christ!"
editorial_note: The translation preserves the mystical identification with all suffering and the repeated address to Christ.
